title: Hands-On Exercise 2
section: Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
text:
Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
This extension is one of the ggplot2 extensions which is designed to combine separate ggplot2 graphs into single figure.
The general syntax that combines graphs are as follows:

2-column layout using the + sign
() to create a subplot group
2-row layout using the / sign


2 graphs combined
The code block below shows how 2 histograms are combined

p1 + p2










3 graphs combined
The code block below does the following to combine 3 plots:

/ stacks 2 ggplot2 graphs
| places the plots beside each other
() defines the sequence of the plotting


(p1 / p2) | p3

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with tags
The package also provides auto-tagging capabilities to identify the subplots in the figure with plot_annotation().

((p1 / p2) | p3) + 
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with insert
The package also allows plots to be placed freely on top/below another plot with inset_element().

p3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Combining both patchwork and ggtheme while creating a composite figure
The code block showcases how both ggtheme and patchwork can be combined.

patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The tooltip aesthetic
The following code chunks below plots the interactive statistical graph using the ggiraph pacakge. This performs the following:

ggplot() object is first created. along with geom_dotplot_interactive() where it generates an interactive version of the graph
girafe() is used to generate an svg object to be displayed on an html page


Tooltip with only Student’s ID

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE, 
    binwidth = 1, 
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, 
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)





When the mouse hovers over the points in the graph above, it will display the student’s ID. This is done by editing in the geom_dotplot_interactive() function, where aes(tooltip = ID).


Displaying multiple information using tooltip

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS)) 

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)





In this code block, where both the student’s ID and the class the student is in are to be displayed, a variable exam_data$tooltip is created in the first 3 lines of code, where it defines how it will be displayed. Afterwards, in the main body of code, tooltip is then assigned to exam_data$tooltip.


Customise your tooltip style

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white; #<<
font-style:bold; color:black;" #<<

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = ID),                   
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(    #<<
    opts_tooltip(    #<<
      css = tooltip_css)) #<<
)                                        





In this code block, the style is changed, where the background colour is while and the font colour and black and bolded.
This is done by introducing the variable tooltip_css, where you will assign the background colour, font style and the colour.
Afterwards, within the girafe() function, there is an additional options, where you would reference the tooltip_css as such there.


Advanced tooltip: displaying statistics
Let’s say that I want to display the 90% confidence interval of the mean of each subjects in the graph below.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
                   aes(x = RACE),
) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS, 
                   tooltip = after_stat(  
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),  
    fun.data = "mean_se", 
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,  
    fill = "light blue"
  ) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2, size = 0.2
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8*0.618)





In the code chunk above, tooltip is referenced in the first 4 lines, where the function is created to calculate the mean scores for the subjects with the intervals, along with how it is going to be displayed.
After that, it is then pointed within stat_summary() as shown in the code chunk.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The data_id aesthetic
Let’s say, I want to identify visually the students in the same class over the histodot graph below.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(           
    aes(data_id = CLASS),             
    stackgroups = TRUE,               
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618                      
)                                        





What is done is that data_id is used within geom_dotplot_interactive() where it referenced CLASS (data_id = CLASS). As such, when the clicker hovers over the dots, the dots will change colour to orange, where it indicates the students that are in the same class. This allows me to visually see the distributions of the students.
It is to note that the default colour for this is orange, where: hover_css = "fill:orange;"

Re-styling the hover effect
Instead of the dot’s colour changing to orange, I would want to highlight the students that are in the same class.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;") 
  )                                        
)                                        





In the code block above, options is introduced within the girafe() function, where you can do the highlighting effect as such.

  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = CLASS, 
        data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")

)                                        





The graph shows how the students in the same class is both highlighted, and shown as the tooltip.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views
In hands-on exercise 2, we came across the use of multiple graphs. This can also be applied in interactive statistical graphs as well.
In this example, I will be displaying the graph of marks for both Maths and Science. When the mouse hovers over a data point in either graph, the corresponding data point on the other visualisation will be highlighted as well.
This is done by:

Using appropriate interactive functions of ggiraph to create the multiple views.
Using patchwork function within the girafe function to create the interactive coordinated multiple views.

The code chunk below showcases that.

p1 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

p2 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(code = print(p1 + p2), 
       width_svg = 6,
       height_svg = 3,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
         )
       ) 





The data_id aesthetic is critical to link observations between both plots, while the tooltip aesthetic is optional but a nice to have to improve the visualisation.

Coordinated Multiple Views with plotly
To create a coordinated linked plot using plotly, 3 steps need to be done:

2 scatterplots will be created using ggplot2 functions

p1 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +

title: Hands-On Exercise 4
text:
Distribution with Ridgeline Plot
A ridgeline plot (or Joyplot) is a technique of data visualisation that reveals the distribution of a numeric value for several groups. The distributions can be represented by using either histograms or density plots, all alligned to the same horizontal scale and presented with a slight overlap.
When are ridgeline plots applicable in explaining our data findings?

They make sense when the number of groups to represent is medium to high, so often a classic window separation takes too much space. When groups overlap each other, it allows the use of space more efficiently. However, if there is < than 5 groups, other forms of distribution plots would be better.
They make sense when there is a clear pattern in the result (i.e. obvious ranking in groups). Else, the groups will overlap one another, leading to a messy plot, making it counter-intuitive.


Plotting the ridgeline with the ggridges method
The ggridges package is one of the ways to build a ridgeline plot. In the package, it provides 2 main geom to do so:

geom_ridgeline(): This function takes height values directly to draw the ridgelines
geom_density_ridges(): This function first estimates the data densities and then draws those using ridgelines

The code chunk below is plotted using geom_density_ridges():

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()










Making the plot more colourful along the x-axis
At times, we would like the area under the ridgelines to be filled with colours that vary in some form along the x-axis. This is achieved by using either geom_ridgeline_gradient() or geom_density_ridges_gradient(). Both functions acts the same as the functions discussed earlier, only with the added effect of varying fill colours. However, they do not allow for alpha transparency in the fill, therefore a choice have to be made: have changing fill colours or transparency.
The code chunk below showcases the effect:

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()

Warning: `stat(x)` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `after_stat(x)` instead.


Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18











Mapping probabilities directly onto colour
The package also provides a statistic function, called stat_density_ridges() that replaces stat_density() of ggplot2. This function plots the ridgeline by mapping the probabilities calculated via the use of stats(ecdf).
The code chunk below uses the function above, which represents the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.

ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18









NOTE: You must include the argument calc_ecdf = TRUE in stat_density_ridges().


Plotting ridgelines quantile-ly
The function geom_density_ridges_gradient() also allows the plot to be coloured by quantile, via the calculated stats(quantile)aesthetic as shown in the figure below.

ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18









We can also specify specific quartiles by cut points like 2.5% or 97.5% tails to colour the plot as shown below.

ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18

title: Hands-On Exercise 4
text:
Distribution using Raincloud Plot
Another data visualisation technique for data distribution would be Raincloud Plot, which produces a half-density to a distribution plot. As the name suggests, the density plot is in the shape of a “raincloud”. This plot enhances the traditional box-plot by highlighting multiple modalities (an indication that groups may exists). A boxplot does not show where the densities are clustered, but a raincloud plot does.
In this part of the exercise, we will be visualising the distribution of English score by race by using the raincloud plot. It will be created by using functions provided by ggdist and ggplot2 packages.

Plot a Half Eye Graph
To plot this graph, we are using the function stat_halfeye() of the ggdist package. This produces the visualisation, which contains a half-density and a slab-interval.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)








In the code chunk above, the slab interval is removed by setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA.


Adding boxplot with geom_boxplot()
We will add the second geometry layer by using the function geom_boxplot() of ggplot2. This will produce a narrow boxplot. We will then reduce the width and adjust the opacity.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)










Adding Dot Plots with stat_dots()
We will add the third geometry layer by using the function stats_dots() of the ggdist package. This will produce a half-dot plot, similar to a histograph that indicates the number of samples (number of dots) in each bin. side = "left" is written to indicate that we cant it on the left-hand side.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)










Finishing it up
The last geometric layer is to use the function coord_flip() of the ggplot2 package. This flips the raincloud chart horizontally to give it the “raincloud’ experience. theme_economist() of the ggthemes package is also added to give the raincloud chart a professional publishing standard look.

ggplot(exam_data, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +

One-sample test: The gghistostats() method
The code chunk below shows how gghistostats() is used to build a visual of one-sample test on English scores.

set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam_data,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores"
)








The following information is given from the test:

Statistical details
Bayes Factor
Sample sizes
Distribution summary


What is Bayes Factor?
Bayes Factor is a measure of the strength of evidence in favour of one hypothesis among two competing hypotheses. This offers a way to evaluate the data in favour of a null hypothesis (H0) & use external information to do so. It also tells us the weight of the evidence in favour of a given hypothesis.
when comparing both alternative (H1) and null (H0) hypotheses, the factor often written as B10. This is defined as follows:
\[
\frac{\text{likelihood of data given } H_1}
{\text{likelihood of data given } H_0}
=
\frac{P(D \mid H_1)}
{P(D \mid H_0)}
\]
The Schwarz criterion is one of the easiest ways to calculate rough approximation of the Bayes Factor.


Interpreting Bayes Factor
The ratio of the factor is positive. Below is a table of common interpretation of the values of the Bayes Factor:



If B10 is…
Then you have…




> 100
Extreme evidence for H1


30 - 100
Very strong evidence for H1


10 - 30
Strong evidence for H1


3 - 10
Moderate evidence for H1


1 - 3
Anecdotal evidence for H1


1
No evidence


1/3 - 1
Anecdotal evidence for H0


1/10 - 1/3
Moderate evidence for H0


1/30 - 1/10
Strong evidence for H0


1/100 - 1/30
Very strong evidence for H0


< 1/100
Extreme evidence for H0

Visualising the uncertainty of point estimates using ggplot2
A point estimate is a single number, like mean. Uncertainty is expressed as a standard error, like confidence interval. Uncertainty of a point estimate IS NOT EQUAL to the variance of a sample!
In this section, we will be plotting error bars of Maths scores by race by using data provided in the exam_data tibble dataframe.
First, the code chunk below will derive the necessary summary statistics:

my_sum <- exam_data %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n=n(),
    mean=mean(MATHS),
    sd=sd(MATHS)
    ) %>%
  mutate(se=sd/sqrt(n-1))

From the code chunk above:

group_by() of the dplyr package is used to group the observation by race
summarise() is used to compute the count, mean and standard deviation of the observations
mutate() is used to derive standard error of Maths by race
The output is then sabled as a tibble data table called my_sum

Error bars are computed bt using the formula mean+/-se
It is important to indicate stat = "identity in the function geom_point()

section: Drawing the lower corner of the scatterplot matrix
text:
Drawing the lower corner of the scatterplot matrix
A correlation matrix is symmetric. This means that the lower half and upper half of the matrix contain the same pairwise relationships, only in opposite positions.
Therefore, it is common to display only one half of the matrix.
The code chunk below removes the upper panel and displays only the lower half of the scatterplot matrix.

pairs(wine_num, 
      upper.panel = NULL)








From the code chunk above:

upper.panel = NULL removes the upper half of the matrix.
This makes the visualisation less crowded.
The lower half is enough to interpret the pairwise relationships.

Similarly, the code chunk below removes the lower panel and displays only the upper half of the scatterplot matrix.

pairs(wine_num, 
      lower.panel = NULL)








From the code chunk above:

lower.panel = NULL removes the lower half of the matrix.
The remaining upper half still contains the same pairwise relationship information.
This is useful when we want a cleaner version of the full scatterplot matrix.

text:
Including correlation coefficients in the scatterplot matrix
Instead of showing only scatterplots, it is also possible to include correlation coefficients in the scatterplot matrix.
First, the code chunk below creates a helper function called panel.cor().

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep = "")
  
  if(missing(cex.cor)) {
    cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt)
  }
  
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

The code chunk below improves the basic correlation matrix by adding aesthetic customisation, hierarchical ordering, title and subtitle.

  ggcorrplot.args = list(

    hc.order = TRUE,

What is added into the code chunk above that improves the visuals of the correlation matrix?

outline.color = "black" adds a clear outline around the matrix cells.
hc.order = TRUE arranges similar variables closer together through hierarchical clustering.
tl.cex = 10 adjusts the text size of the variable labels.
title and subtitle are used to improve the context of the visualisation.

Customising the text size
At times, we may want to adjust the text size of the correlation matrix to improve readability.
The code chunk below shows how this can be done by using ggplot.component.

      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),

    )

use = "complete.obs" ensures that only complete observations are used.
The computed correlation matrix is saved as wine_cor.

Getting started with corrplot()
The code chunk below plots the corrgram using the default settings of corrplot().

corrplot(wine_cor)








From the plot generated:

The default visual object is a circle.
The default layout is a full symmetric matrix.
The default colour scheme uses a diverging colour scale.
Positive correlations and negative correlations are shown using different colours.
Stronger correlations are represented by darker and larger symbols.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Working with visual geometrics
The corrplot package supports several visual geometrics through the method argument. Examples include:

"circle"
"square"
"ellipse"
"number"
"shade"
"color"
"pie"

The code chunk below changes the visual geometry from the default circle to ellipse.

corrplot(wine_cor,
         method = "ellipse")








What can we learn from this makeover?

method = "ellipse" changes how the correlation values are encoded.
The shape and direction of the ellipse help to show the strength and direction of the correlation.
Different methods can be used depending on the intended visual emphasis.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Working with layout
The corrplot() function supports three main layout types:

"full"
"upper"
"lower"

The default layout is "full", which shows the full correlation matrix. Since the correlation matrix is symmetric, it is often cleaner to show only the upper or lower half.

cor_mtest <- function(mat, conf.level = 0.95) {

  colnames(uppCI.mat) <- rownames(uppCI.mat) <- colnames(mat)

}

    x = 0.1, y = 1,

    align = "center",

    title = txt,
    tickformat = ".0%",
    tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

axis() creates a reusable formatting object for each ternary axis.

  a = ~YOUNG_PROP,
  b = ~ACTIVE_PROP,
  c = ~OLD_PROP,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(size = 6,
                color = "black"),
  text = ~paste("Year:", Year,
                "<br>Young:", round(YOUNG_PROP * 100, 1), "%",
                "<br>Economically Active:", round(ACTIVE_PROP * 100, 1), "%",
                "<br>Old:", round(OLD_PROP * 100, 1), "%"),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    annotations = label("Population Structure, 2018"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes
  )

a, b and c are used instead of the usual x and y aesthetics.
mode = "markers" displays the observations as points.
marker controls the size and colour of the plotted points.
text defines the information that appears when the user hovers over a point.
layout() adds the annotation label and ternary axis settings.

This interactive version is more useful for exploration because the exact composition can be inspected using the hover tooltip.

data.matrix() converts the selected numerical data into matrix format.
The output matrix is saved as wh_matrix.
The row names are retained as country names.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Plotting a basic heatmap without clustering
text:
Plotting a basic heatmap without clustering
The code chunk below creates a basic heatmap without row and column dendrograms.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      Rowv = NA,
                      Colv = NA)








From the code chunk above:

heatmap() is used to create the static heatmap.
Rowv = NA removes row clustering.
Colv = NA removes column clustering.

This produces a heatmap that follows the original row and column order of the matrix. It is useful when we want to inspect the raw layout of the data before applying any clustering.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Plotting a clustered heatmap
By default, heatmap() produces a clustered heatmap. This means that the rows and columns are reordered based on similarity.
The code chunk below creates a clustered heatmap using the default settings.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix)








From the generated heatmap, there are 2 things to note:

The rows and columns are reordered based on clustering.
Dendrograms are shown to indicate the similarity structure between rows and columns.

A clustered heatmap is useful because it helps to identify groups of countries and indicators that have similar patterns.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Scaling the heatmap by column
When variables are measured on different scales, some variables may dominate the heatmap. For example, one variable may have much larger values than another variable. This makes it difficult to compare patterns across variables.
To address this issue, the data can be scaled by column.
The code chunk below normalises the matrix column-wise.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale = "column",
                      cexRow = 0.6,
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))








What can we learn from this makeover?

scale = "column" standardises the variables by column.
cexRow = 0.6 reduces the font size of the row labels.
cexCol = 0.8 adjusts the font size of the column labels.
margins = c(10, 4) gives more space for the axis labels.

This version is more useful for comparing variables because the values are placed on a more comparable scale.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Building a basic interactive heatmap
The code chunk below creates a basic interactive heatmap using heatmaply().

heatmaply(wh_matrix)

ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

Studying both the code chunk and the interactive heatmap that is generated, there are 3 things to note:

heatmaply() automatically creates an interactive heatmap.
Row labels are placed on the right side of the heatmap by default.
The dendrograms help to show how observations and variables are clustered.

This interactive heatmap allows users to inspect cell values more closely by hovering over the visualisation.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Scaling method
Scaling is suitable when the variables are assumed to come from distributions that can be compared using standardised values. It subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation.
The code chunk below scales the variable values column-wise.

heatmaply(wh_matrix,
          scale = "column")





From the code chunk above:

scale = "column" applies scaling to each variable.
Each value is interpreted relative to its column mean and standard deviation.
This makes variables more comparable across columns.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Normalising method
Normalising is useful when the variables have different ranges and do not necessarily follow a normal distribution. It brings the values into a 0 to 1 scale.
The code chunk below applies the normalising method before plotting the heatmap.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix))





From the code chunk above:

normalize() rescales the values into a comparable range.
The original shape of the distribution is still preserved.
This is useful when the goal is to compare relative patterns across variables.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Percentising method
Percentising converts the values into empirical percentiles. This is similar to ranking, but the values are expressed as the proportion of observations that fall at or below a given value.
The code chunk below applies the percentising method before plotting the heatmap.

heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix))





From the code chunk above:

percentize() converts the values into empirical percentile values.
Each value becomes easier to interpret as a relative position.
This is useful when we want to compare each country against the distribution of all countries.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Manual approach
In the manual approach, the distance measure and clustering method are selected by the analyst.
The code chunk below creates a heatmap using Euclidean distance and Ward’s method.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D")





From the code chunk above:

dist_method = "euclidean" calculates dissimilarity using Euclidean distance.
hclust_method = "ward.D" applies Ward’s hierarchical clustering method.
normalize(wh_matrix) ensures that the values are comparable before clustering.

This approach is useful when the analyst already has a suitable clustering method in mind.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Statistical approach
Instead of choosing the clustering method manually, we can use statistical support to compare clustering methods.
The code chunk below computes the distance matrix for the normalised World Happiness data.

wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix),
             method = "euclidean")

The next code chunk uses dend_expend() to compare clustering methods.

dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6641312
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6455811
3      unknown         single 0.4676511
4      unknown       complete 0.5668585
5      unknown        average 0.7181243
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.6575001
7      unknown         median 0.6210611
8      unknown       centroid 0.6871334


From the output table:

different hierarchical clustering methods are compared
the optim value is used to assess the quality of each method
the method with the higher optimum value is usually preferred

The next code chunk uses the average linkage method to create a hierarchical clustering object.

wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d,
                   method = "average")

After deciding on the clustering method, the next step is to determine the number of clusters.

num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)

plot(num_k)








From the plot generated, we can inspect the suggested number of clusters. If the result suggests that three clusters are suitable, this can be reflected in the heatmap.
The code chunk below creates the interactive heatmap using the statistical clustering results.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)





What can we learn from the statistical approach?

The distance matrix is computed first.
Different clustering methods are compared using dend_expend().
find_k() helps to identify a suitable number of clusters.
The selected clustering method and number of clusters are then used in heatmaply().

Applying Optimal Leaf Ordering
The code chunk below applies Optimal Leaf Ordering to the heatmap.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix),
          seriate = "OLO")





From the code chunk above:

seriate = "OLO" applies Optimal Leaf Ordering.
The ordering is chosen to reduce dissimilarity between adjacent leaves.
This can make the heatmap pattern easier to read.

Applying Gruvaeus and Wainer ordering

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix),

Applying mean ordering
The code chunk below applies mean ordering.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix),
          seriate = "mean")





From the code chunk above:

seriate = "mean" orders the values based on their mean.
This provides an alternative ordering approach.
It may be useful when we want a simpler ordering rule.

Turning seriation off
The code chunk below turns off seriation.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix),
          seriate = "none")





From the code chunk above:

This allows us to compare the effect of seriation against the non-seriated heatmap.
It is useful for checking how much the ordering method changes the visual pattern.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Plotting a basic parallel coordinates plot
text:
Plotting a basic parallel coordinates plot
The code chunk below creates a basic static parallel coordinates plot using the selected World Happiness variables.

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12))








Studying both the code chunk and the plot that is generated, there are 2 things to note:

data = wh tells R to use the World Happiness dataset.
columns = c(7:12) selects the numerical variables that will be shown as the parallel axes.

Although this basic plot shows the structure of the data, it is difficult to interpret because the lines overlap heavily. The variables may also be measured on different scales, which makes direct comparison harder.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Aesthetic makeover #1: adding grouping, scaling and boxplot
text:
Aesthetic makeover #1: adding grouping, scaling and boxplot
The basic plot can be improved by adding grouping, scaling, transparency and boxplots. This makes it easier to compare patterns across regions.
The code chunk below shows how this is done:

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Variables")

Warning: The following aesthetics were dropped during statistical transformation:
colour.
ℹ This can happen when ggplot fails to infer the correct grouping structure in
  the data.
ℹ Did you forget to specify a `group` aesthetic or to convert a numerical
  variable into a factor?









What can we learn from this makeover?

groupColumn = 2 colours the lines based on the second column in the dataset, which represents the region.
scale = "uniminmax" rescales each selected variable so that its minimum value becomes 0 and its maximum value becomes 1.
alphaLines = 0.2 reduces the opacity of the lines so that overlapping lines are less visually overwhelming.
boxplot = TRUE adds boxplots to each variable axis.
title adds a descriptive title to the plot.

The scaling step is important because parallel coordinates plots compare multiple variables on the same visual space. Without scaling, variables with larger numerical ranges may dominate the visual interpretation.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Aesthetic makeover #2: creating small multiples by region
text:
Aesthetic makeover #2: creating small multiples by region
Since ggparcoord() extends the ggplot2 framework, it can be combined with other ggplot2 functions. One useful option is to use facet_wrap() to create one plot for each region.
The code chunk below creates multiple parallel coordinates plots by region.

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)








From the code chunk above:

facet_wrap(~ Region) creates one small multiple plot for each geographical region.
This allows the multivariate pattern of countries to be compared within each region.
It also reduces the problem of having too many lines in a single plot.

This version is useful when the goal is to compare regional patterns. However, some of the x-axis labels may overlap because the variable names are long.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Aesthetic makeover #3: rotating x-axis text labels
text:
Aesthetic makeover #3: rotating x-axis text labels
To improve readability, the x-axis labels can be rotated by using the theme() function from ggplot2.
The code chunk below rotates the x-axis labels by 30 degrees.

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))








What is added into the code chunk above that improves the visuals of the plot?

theme() is used to customise the appearance of the plot.
axis.text.x refers specifically to the x-axis text labels.
element_text(angle = 30) rotates the labels by 30 degrees.

This makes the variable names easier to read, especially when the plot contains several long axis labels.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Aesthetic makeover #4: adjusting rotated x-axis text labels
text:
Aesthetic makeover #4: adjusting rotated x-axis text labels
Rotating the x-axis labels improves readability, but the labels may still overlap with the plot area. This can be improved by adjusting the horizontal justification of the text.
The code chunk below rotates and adjusts the x-axis labels.

ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))








From the code chunk above:

angle = 30 rotates the labels.
hjust = 1 adjusts the horizontal position of the labels.
The combination helps to reduce overlap between the text labels and the plot area.

This final static version is more readable because it combines scaling, grouping, faceting and axis label adjustment.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Building a basic interactive parallel coordinates plot
text:
Building a basic interactive parallel coordinates plot
The code chunk below creates a basic interactive parallel coordinates plot.

parallelPlot(wh_parallel,
             width = 320,
             height = 250)





Studying the code chunk above:

parallelPlot() is used to create the interactive parallel coordinates plot.

This plot allows users to interact with the parallel coordinates display. However, some of the axis labels may still be difficult to read because they are long.

Rotating the axis labels
The code chunk below rotates the axis labels by using the rotateTitle argument.

parallelPlot(wh_parallel,
             rotateTitle = TRUE)





From the code chunk above:

rotateTitle = TRUE rotates the axis titles.
This helps to reduce overlap between the variable names.
The plot becomes easier to use when the variables have longer labels.

One useful interactive feature of parallelPlot() is that a user can click on a variable axis. Once a variable is selected, the line colour changes according to the values of that variable. This makes it easier to inspect how high and low values flow across the other axes.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Changing the colour scheme
The default colour scheme can be changed by using the continuousCS argument. This is useful when we want the colour gradient to better support the interpretation of high and low values.
The code chunk below changes the continuous colour scheme.

parallelPlot(wh_parallel,
             continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
             rotateTitle = TRUE)





What can we learn from this makeover?

continuousCS = "YlOrRd" changes the continuous colour scale to a yellow-orange-red palette.
rotateTitle = TRUE keeps the axis labels readable.
The colour gradient helps to highlight the selected variable more clearly when the plot is explored interactively.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Adding histograms to the parallel coordinates plot
text:
Adding histograms to the parallel coordinates plot
Another useful feature of parallelPlot() is the ability to show histograms along the axes. This helps users understand the distribution of values for each variable.
The code chunk below creates a logical vector to turn on histogram visibility for all variables.

histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh_parallel))

The code chunk below adds histograms to the interactive parallel coordinates plot.

parallelPlot(wh_parallel,
             rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisibility)





From the code chunk above:

rep(TRUE, ncol(wh_parallel)) creates a vector of TRUE values for all columns in the selected dataset.
histoVisibility = histoVisibility turns on the histogram display for all selected variables.
The histograms help to show the distribution of values along each variable axis.

This interactive version is useful because it combines multivariate comparison with distribution information.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
section: Grouped summaries without using the pipe
text:
Grouped summaries without using the pipe
The code chunk below shows how grouped summaries can be created without using the pipe operator.

realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018,
                               `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`,
                               `Planning Area`,
                               `Property Type`,
                               `Type of Sale`)

realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped,
                                   `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   .groups = "drop")

From the code chunk above:

group_by() is used to group the transaction records by project and geographic hierarchy.
summarise() is used to calculate the summary measures for each group.
sum() is used to calculate the total number of units sold and total area.
median() is used to calculate the median unit price and median transacted price.
na.rm = TRUE removes missing values before the calculations are performed.

Although this method works, it requires intermediate data frames to be created. This can make the workflow longer than necessary.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Building a basic treemap
The code chunk below creates a basic treemap using the treemap() function.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")








Studying both the code chunk and the treemap that is generated, there are 3 things to note:

index defines the hierarchy used in the treemap.
vSize maps the size of each rectangle to Total Unit Sold.
vColor identifies the variable that can be used for colouring the rectangles.

However, the colour mapping in the basic treemap may not represent median unit price correctly. This is because the type argument has not been defined. When type is not stated, the function may colour the rectangles based on the hierarchy instead of the numerical variable.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
Working with vColor and type
To ensure that the rectangle colours represent the numerical values in vColor, the type argument should be specified.
The code chunk below uses type = "value".

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")








What can we learn from this makeover?

type = "value" tells the function to colour the rectangles based on the numerical values in vColor.
Higher and lower median unit prices are shown using different colour intensities.
The legend now becomes meaningful because it describes the range of median unit prices.

This version is more appropriate when the purpose of the treemap is to compare both the number of units sold and the median unit price.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
The value type treemap
The code chunk below creates a value type treemap using the RdYlBu palette.

        type = "value",
        palette = "RdYlBu",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")








From the code chunk above:

palette = "RdYlBu" applies a diverging colour palette.
type = "value" maps median unit price to colour.
Since median unit price is always positive, one side of the diverging palette may not be fully used.

This is useful to note because a diverging palette is usually more suitable when the data has a meaningful centre, such as zero.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5
text:
The manual type treemap
The code chunk below creates a manual type treemap using the same diverging palette.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",

        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)")








What can we learn from the code chunk above?

type = "manual" maps the data range more directly to the chosen palette.
A diverging palette may become confusing when the variable is only positive.
This is because viewers may interpret opposite colours as having opposite meanings, even when the data does not contain negative values.

To avoid this issue, a sequential palette can be used instead.

From the code chunk above:

palette = "Blues" applies a sequential colour palette.
Sequential palettes are more suitable when the variable moves from low to high.
This makes the treemap easier to interpret because darker and lighter shades represent different price levels.

The layout is designed to produce rectangles with more balanced shapes.
This can improve readability when there are many small categories.

title: Hands-On Exercise 5

Adding boundary lines
When a treemap has multiple hierarchy levels, boundary lines can help distinguish between groups.
The code chunk below adds boundary lines for planning region and planning area.

ggplot(data = realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "gray40",
                                size = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "gray20") +
  labs(title = "Resale Condominium Treemap with Hierarchical Boundaries, 2018",
       fill = "Median Unit Price")








What is added into the code chunk above that improves the visuals of the treemap?

geom_treemap_subgroup2_border() adds boundary lines for the second hierarchy level.
geom_treemap_subgroup_border() adds boundary lines for the first hierarchy level.
The boundaries make the hierarchy clearer and improve interpretability.

Creating an interactive treemap
The code chunk below uses d3tree() to create an interactive treemap.

if (requireNamespace("d3treeR", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(d3treeR)
  d3tree(tm, rootname = "Singapore")
} else {
  message("The d3treeR package is not installed. Run the installation code above before creating the interactive treemap.")
}





From the code chunk above:

requireNamespace() checks whether d3treeR is installed.
library(d3treeR) loads the package when it is available.
d3tree() converts the treemap object into an interactive treemap.
rootname = "Singapore" defines the root label of the hierarchy.

This interactive version is useful because the viewer can explore the hierarchy more directly.
